items.echo: her name, said at the top
items.lethe: the water of Lethe, in his hands

episodes: Traveller… does this hill have an end?
…Merope?
Merope. A beautiful name. Is it mine?
Yours. In Corinth I called you by it for forty years.
I don't remember. Everyone who comes here drinks from the river. I must have drunk too.
Lethe. They stole you from me too.
No one stole me. There is only an emptiness where my name should be.
Zeus! Take back your stone, take back your hill, take anything. Only give her back to me!
Don't shout. Voices don't carry here. Does the sky open at the top? Down here it is always ash-grey. When you climb, tell me about the stars.
It does. There are stars. Seven sisters: the Pleiades. One is fainter than the rest.
Why fainter?
She married a mortal. She dimmed her light for shame, they say. Her name is Merope.
Merope… My name. A mortal… Are you that mortal?
Don't answer. “Corinth” makes something ache in me. The air never moves here. Bring me wind from the top.
At the top the wind comes off the sea. It smells of salt. Corinth had two seas; our palace looked on both.
I used to come home by sea. Every morning you stood at the eastern gate and counted the ships into harbour.
The ships… I was waiting for someone. Always someone.
When I remember who, I'll tell you. But those mornings feel as if they never ended.
You know me, and I don't know you. What is your name, traveller?
Sisyphus.
Sisyphus… Nothing. A stone dropped in water makes more rings than that.
In Corinth, every door opened at that name.
Don't grieve. Not even my name meant anything. I had to hear it from you.
Your voice is hoarse. You shouted again up there.
At Zeus. I'll shout until he hears.
Here, shouts reach only the stone. And the stone rolls them back to you.
Is it cold up there? Bring me snow. I want to remember what cold was.
I brought you a handful of snow. …It melted on the way.
Merope touches his wet palm.
Cold. I know this: mountain cold. My father's mountain.
Kyllene, in Arcadia. You were born there.
Kyllene. Even the name is cool in my mouth.
There are voices in my ears. Six women, laughing. They have no faces.
Your sisters. Maia, Elektra, Taygete, Alkyone, Kelaino, Sterope.
Say them again. …No. Only the first.
Maia.
Maia. Hers is the nearest voice. I think she used to braid my hair.
Today at the top I didn't shout at Zeus. I called on Hermes.
Who is Hermes?
The guide of the dead. He is the one who dragged me here. Maia's son — your nephew.
My nephew… What did you say to him?
I offered a bargain. I push the stone for ever, without one complaint. In exchange, your memory.
What did he answer?
The wind answered. And the stone, rolling down.
You speak to gods like a merchant.
I've sold to them before.
It shows. There's still haggling in your voice.
What did you do, when you were alive?
I built Corinth: its walls, its two harbours. Whatever crossed between the two seas paid me first.
You speak of walls with pride. Was I inside them?
Always.
A smell keeps following me. I can't tell where from; nothing here has a smell.
Something warm. On a stone, in the sun.
Does anything grow up there? Pick it and bring it to me.
Thyme. It grows between the stones, pressed flat by the wind.
This. This was it. A hill… a house on the hill. A terrace.
The slope of Acrocorinth. Our terrace smelled of thyme.
There was a loom on the terrace. My hands remember it better than I do.
On that loom I was weaving a cloth. Deep blue, with seven stars on it.
I don't know who it was for.
For me. I lost it at sea, on a voyage.
A pity. I wove the seventh star in pale thread. That much I remember.
Where did Corinth's water come from?
From Peirene, a spring on Acrocorinth. Before, there was no water there; the rock was bone-dry.
I bargained with the river-god Asopos. He made the rock give water.
And what did you pay?
A secret.
Autolykos the thief stole my cattle. He changed their colour, and no one could prove a thing.
So I carved into their hooves: “Stolen by Autolykos.” The tracks led straight to his barn.
Into the hooves? You made the thief read his own name?
Merope laughs. Sisyphus stops where he stands.
For forty years I came home for that sound.
There's something I don't understand. My sisters married gods. Why did I marry a mortal?
You chose. It was a feast on Kyllene, and gods were there too. You got up, came over, and sat down beside me.
Why? Why you?
You said, “You're the only one here who isn't afraid of anything.”
That's not a reason to love.
It's a reason to fear.
You weren't afraid that night.
Perhaps I saved the fear for later.
Sisyphus's palms are bleeding.
The stone slipped twice. Damn Zeus.
Your anger keeps you warm. Nothing does, down here.
When the first light strikes the top, take it in your hands. Bring it to me.
Dawn. I held it in my hands, look… it's fading.
I can see your face. Clearly, for the first time.
You're old.
I lived a long time.
Longer than me?
Did we have children?
…A son. Glaukos.
Glaukos. A warm name in my mouth. Like bread.
Where is he now? Did he grow up?
He grew up.
There's a small hand in mine. It smells of horses.
Glaukos. He loved horses more than people. He'd fall asleep in the stables.
I fetched him from the stables every evening, didn't I? Straw all through his hair.
You did.
Do the dead sleep? I have never slept here.
I'd like to dream, once. Glaukos, the terrace that smelled of thyme.
Bring me something from up there that brings sleep.
A poppy. Below the summit, among the stones, this one alone had opened.
Red. The only colour down here.
There was red somewhere. A lot of red. On sand.
The colour leaves Sisyphus's face.
Yesterday I saw fear on your face. On the face of a man who shouts at gods.
It was nothing.
It was something.
I'll bring everything back, Merope. The good things first. The rest… later.
Sisyphus comes down, his lip split, his eyes burning.
Today I spat at the sky. I'll push this stone and push it, until the sky tears.
And if you tore it, what would fall out?
I don't know! I don't need to know. Let it tear.
Rage is a kind of hope, Sisyphus.
Hope? I hope for nothing.
No one spits at an empty sky. You still think there's someone up there to hit.
Sisyphus doesn't answer. He turns back to his stone, with hard steps.
I want to know one thing: does anything from up there reach down here?
Shout my name from the top. I told you not to shout, I know. This time, shout for me.
I shouted. Your name struck from hill to hill and came back. Did you hear?
Not a sound.
But something happened. As if someone had called me from another room… I turned my head.
Which room?
I don't know. It had no door.
I remember a gate. Its bronze ring was cold in my hand in the mornings.
My hand was always on it, ready to open. For whom?
The stone pulled to the left today. Three times. It never used to.
I asked about a gate. You told me about a stone.
The chained man up the hill gave men fire. He is still paying. What did you give?
Water. To a city.
You told me you paid for it with a secret. Was that all?
The secret was only the first payment. The rest was everything after.
The man in the pool looks at me as if he knows me. As if I owed him something.
Tantalus. Your sister Dione's husband.
Dione… One more sister. Her husband in a pool, mine on a hill.
Atlas's daughters, it seems, chose their husbands badly.
The snow melted. The light faded. Your voice never arrived. Everything you bring dies in my hand.
The only thing up there that lasts is stone.
Then bring me stone. As much as fits in my palm.
A pebble from the top. It lay beside my stone; perhaps it broke off it.
This is what you push? This small?
A little bigger.
But it's heavy. The first thing that has weight in my hand. I'll keep it.
The shades whisper of a mortal who tricked the queen of the dead and went back up.
That was me.
You say it with pride. What did you tell her?
That someone had wronged me. Queens cannot bear an injustice.
He walks on without saying who.
I've found a way. Lethe has an opposite: the lake of Mnemosyne. Memory. Whoever drinks from it gets everything back.
Who told you that?
There's an old saying among the shades: “Do not drink from the spring by the white cypress. Drink the cold water of the lake of Memory.”
They say the gods leave no doors. I always found one. I'll find that lake, and bring you its water in my hands.
Say you bring it. Say I drink. Everything comes back.
Corinth comes back. The sea, your loom, Glaukos. I come back.
And if what I remember is not what you want me to remember?
Something crosses Sisyphus's face, and is gone.
You'll remember. I'll tell you the rest.
You always do the telling.
I searched the top stone by stone. No lake. Only rock and wind.
They've built a wall and called it the sky.
Today I shoved the stone off the top myself. Before they could take it.
What changed?
Nothing. It was at the bottom again. So was I.
You fight the gods to get me back. You search the top stone by stone.
Who wanted me, when I was there?
Sisyphus opens his mouth. Nothing comes.
I don't know. I'm really asking.
The chained man's eagle passes every day at the same hour. Its shadow cuts the plain in two.
Bring me one of its feathers. I want to know with my own hand what cruelty feels like.
It fell as the eagle rose. The chained man's blood is still on the tip.
It's soft. Cruelty is soft? I thought it would cut.
Cruel things are always soft at first.
You said that like someone who knows.
I remember a feast. Torches, a flute in the courtyard. I was dancing.
Our first year. You kicked off a sandal, and half of Corinth went looking for it.
You found it. You brought it back wearing it.
I laughed. Remembering that is… good.
When Glaukos was born there were women in the room. The midwife, neighbours. You weren't there.
I was at the Isthmus. Ships, tolls, a dispute.
A son was being born, and you were counting ships.
It was business.
A lamp burned in the window. Every night. I trimmed the wick. I poured the oil.
I don't know whom I lit it for. But I will.
For a moment, Sisyphus's steps slow.
You brought me the wind, the salt. You can't bring me the sea itself, I know.
But you can look. Today, look at the sea from the top, and tell me its colour.
Green by the shore, violet farther out. Between them a band the colour of wine; the wind turns there.
You describe it like a man who often left by it.
Those who leave know the open sea. Those who stay know the shore.
Did I ever tell you? I chained Death with his own chains. For weeks no one died.
No one died? Then no one could rest.
You were married to the man who chained Death, Merope! Be a little proud.
Sisyphus laughs. Merope does not.
The shades say that when you were brought down the second time, Death was black with rage.
Why a second time? A man dies once.
Sisyphus is silent. He says nothing the rest of the way down.
I know this silence. I have heard it before.
There's something under the emptiness. Like a stone under water: I can't see it, but my foot strikes it.
The dead don't dream.
Tomorrow I'll tell you a dream. If I have one.
You said the dead don't dream. I did.
A man on his deathbed was gripping my hand, whispering: “Don't bury me. Whatever happens, don't bury me.”
So I didn't. And all Corinth spat at me. The woman who left her husband to the dogs, they called me.
That man was you. Wasn't it?
Yes.
Why?
Sisyphus does not answer.
Then tell me this. Did you come back?
I came back. To live. Not to you.
I remember now. I was waiting for you. Every morning. I grew old at that gate.
I was living. I wanted to live every day I had stolen from Death.
I paid for those days. Every one of them.
Remembering is heavy. They say there's a spring past the place where the stone stops: Lethe's source.
You always look at the stone. This time, look past it. For me.
It's there. Just past where the stone stops, under a white cypress.
The water is so still it reflects nothing.
One sip, and the pain would stop. I'd forget you again.
Don't.
Why? For my sake, or for yours?
Because you'd forget me again. All these climbs, everything I brought you, for nothing.
Snow, light, a pebble. So they were loans.
Merope weighs the pebble in her palm.
After you came back, how long did you live?
Years.
How many?
I didn't count. My beard went white.
Where?
In Corinth. In the palace.
And where was I?
In the house by the gate.
Merope looks at her hands for a long time. The pebble is still in her palm.
The same city. Inside the same walls.
I went on counting ships. For years, every morning.
You were up the hill, in the palace. I knew.
I counted them anyway.
I thought Hermes would look for me first at your door. So I kept away.
From me you hid. From Death you hid. Whom did you not hide from, Sisyphus?
The harbour. The market. I walked among the crowds.
So all Corinth saw you. Only I did not.
I remember the cloth with the seven stars. I gave it to you for a journey; nights are cold at sea.
Then I saw it in the agora, on Autolykos's shoulders. I knew it by the pale seventh star.
You said you lost it at sea.
I lied. I gave it to him, to buy a truce.
Two words. That's all it ever took.
The cloth went to Autolykos. And you, I think, to his house.
His daughter's name was Antikleia.
They say the cleverest man in Greece, Odysseus, has your eyes.
So they say.
You don't deny it.
This time I won't lie. I don't know the truth of it myself.
One son grew up in my house, another in someone else's. You were in neither.
Tell me nothing more today. I won't ask.
When he comes down, Merope does not raise her head.
Go.
You asked what Peirene cost. I saw Zeus carry off Aigina, and I sold it to her father, Asopos.
And the girl? What became of her?
I don't know. I never asked.
The water I drank all my life was paid for with a girl.
Every morning I filled my jar at Peirene.
One evening a tall man came to the door and asked for you. I took him for a creditor.
He's out, I said. It was Death.
That evening was your gift to me.
Two words. That's all it took from me, too.
I remember the old woman next door. She moaned for weeks. She couldn't die.
Soldiers came back from the war with their bellies split. They couldn't die either.
I chained Death. I didn't think past that.
Past that, there was me. I sat beside them.
Then Ares came and set Death free. Death took you first.
I was at your bedside. You pulled my hand and bent to my ear.
“Don't bury me.”
I thought it was love. I thought you didn't want to go below without me.
For years I lived on that. A dying man's last wish. Of me.
It was a trick.
Merope begins to say something, and stops.
It was all I had. You've taken that back too.
I kept my word. In the agora they threw stones at me. The first one struck my forehead.
The priests turned my offerings away. Nothing from the wife of an unburied man.
I heard.
Merope lifts her fingers to one spot on her forehead. She still knows the place.
No one weeps here. The tears must have run into Lethe too.
I want to weep, and I can't.
Bring me something from the top that weeps.
In the mornings the stones at the top weep. I caught a drop for you; look.
Stones don't weep. They sweat. Like you.
Did you never see me weep?
Once. When one of your ships went down. For the cargo.
Below, I stood before Persephone. My wife has not buried me, I said: no coin in my mouth, no offering.
I wept. I wept well that day.
Let me go up, I said, and punish her. Then I'll come back on my own feet.
And she believed you.
She did. Because you really hadn't buried me. Because you had kept your word.
You used me as a key, Sisyphus. You opened the door and left the key in the lock.
And when you came back up, did you come to punish me?
No.
That is worse. A punishment is at least a look.
They say I dimmed my light for shame.
Not for shame. So that my sisters would not have to look away from me.
They looked away anyway. And you went off to live.
My father Atlas carries the sky. He can never set it down, or everything falls.
My husband carries a stone.
I carried you.
The gods cheated. Zeus stole girls; I only told. I spoke to them in their own tongue.
Gods cheat because they cannot die. Nothing ever costs them anything.
What was your excuse?
I was going to die.
Everyone was going to die. Not everyone did what you did.
Hermes came to my gate. My sister Maia's son, in his winged sandals.
“Aunt,” he said, “he has gone where you cannot follow.”
What did you say to him?
I laughed. At last, I thought.
Then I shut the gate.
I kept a lamp lit in the window every night, for years. I carried the oil up from the market myself.
I remember the night I put it out. No storm, no news.
I looked at it, and blew.
What year was it?
I don't know. I stopped counting that night too.
Glaukos grew up. In every race, his horses won.
When Pelias died there were funeral games at Iolkos. He took his mares and went; I waved from the gate.
Were you there?
No.
I remember something else: a child laughing among horses.
Then dust on the road. I thought it was you, coming at last. It was a rider from Iolkos.
Glaukos. Our son.
What happened to him? I heard it from the rider. I want to hear it from you.
His own horses tore him apart, at the games. I wasn't there that day either. I was at the harbour; a ship had come in.
A ship.
You bought him those mares. From Thessaly, the best there were.
That was the red I saw. The sand at Iolkos.
For a long time neither speaks. At the foot of the slope, the stone waits.
Who buried Glaukos?
You did.
Alone?
Yes.
I buried my son, and not my husband. Corinth remembered only the second.
Glaukos had a son. Bellerophon. I held him when he was a baby.
He grew up. He rode a winged horse, Pegasos. He flew as high as the sky.
You had a grandson who flew, Sisyphus. And you never even saw him walk.
Sisyphus looks up at the sky. He says nothing.
I push this stone every day, Merope. Every day, again. Isn't my punishment enough?
Your punishment is for the gods. Not for me.
Your pushing gives me nothing back. It only keeps your hands busy.
I died in winter. The hearth was out; only the wall by the gate kept off the wind.
The market women buried me. Some had thrown stones. One had flour on her hands.
I heard. The new shades told of it.
That day I pushed the stone. Like any other day.
Tomorrow I'll ask you a question. Only one.
Ask it now.
No. Tonight, up there, learn to say the answer without dressing it.
You'll tell the truth. For once, and get nothing for it.
I said I would ask you something. This time you'll tell me the truth.
When you were cheating Death, when you said goodbye to me… did you ever think what would become of me?
No.
You rage at the gods. For your stone, for your hill. They gave you the stone, yes. But you earned it.
You carved this stone yourself. A little more with every lie.
Merope—
Don't call me that. You killed that woman. Lethe only buried her.
Merope turns her back on him.
You've turned your back. Perhaps that's easier: what I couldn't say to your face, I'll say to your back.
I'll tell you the rest. All of it. You don't have to listen.
Merope doesn't move. But she doesn't leave either.
At the top today I thought it again: if Zeus hadn't condemned me to this stone, I would—
He cannot finish the sentence.
You would what?
Her back is to him. In her hanging hand is the pebble he brought from the top, her fingers closed on it.
Sisyphus almost speaks. He doesn't; he walks on.
Do you know what I felt when Hermes took me by the collar? Not anger.
Relief. For years I had started at every knock on the door.
At last, I thought.
The first time I pushed the stone, I thought it was the gods' cruelty. With every step I named one of them.
Today I push, and I don't know whose cruelty it is.
Was any of it for me? A single thing?
The wall by the gate. I had it built so the north wind wouldn't batter the house. I chose its stones myself.
I never told you. I told the masons not to say it came from me.
Merope says nothing.
I'm not asking forgiveness. I'm only telling you.
He waits a moment. Her back does not stir, and he goes on.
At the top today my mouth was open. I was only breathing.
When the anger goes, it leaves a hollow. Bigger than the stone.
Again today I stood at the top and didn't shout at the gods. There's no one left to shout at. There's only me.
I told you “Don't.” Not for your sake. For mine.
I'm sorry, Merope. I know it brings nothing back. I'm sorry anyway.
Merope's shoulders stir for a moment. She does not turn.
Words. You were always good with words.
Words got you past Persephone. Past me, too.
You're right. And that is a word too, I know.
Then I'll be quiet.
He passes her without a word.
Merope listens until his footsteps reach the stone.
Sisyphus passes in silence, his eyes on the path.
For the first time Merope looks over her shoulder. Not at his face; at his hands.
He doesn't see. She faces away again.
You've stopped talking.
It's louder this way. Your breath, your footsteps, your stone.
Sisyphus comes down, and is about to pass Merope in silence once more.
Stop.
Merope turns round. Her face is as it was the day she turned away; only her eyes are tired.
I counted the days you were silent. The way I counted ships. That is enough.
What shall I tell you?
Tell me about Corinth. Not about you. Corinth.
Where shall I begin?
The market. The smell of bread. Anywhere you weren't.
Fishmongers at the south end of the agora, bakers at the north. Mornings smell of bread first, then salt.
The bakers… Kleo. When no one would sell me anything, she left bread at my door.
The floury hands among those who buried me were hers. She never threw a stone.
I never heard her name.
Now you have.
I've thought about why I chose you. Because you weren't afraid, you said.
The real reason is this: I was afraid of everything. The sky my father carried, my sisters' eyes.
So I sold you fearlessness.
And I bought it. Without even haggling.
When Death came to the door, I lied to him. While the stones fell, I kept my word not to bury you.
I thought I did it all because of you. I didn't.
I wanted to be the one who obeyed. It was the only way I felt I mattered.
You were the only one in that city who kept a promise.
In Corinth that was worth nothing.
It was worth something to me. I knew its worth. That's why I used it.
And I hated myself for it.
Hating you would have been easier. But the promise was mine, and so was the keeping.
That was the stone I carried. No one saw it, because it never rolled.
Every time, I think the top will change something. It never does. And still I go.
Why?
I don't know yet.
When you do, tell me first.
Do you still hate them, the gods?
I don't think of them any more. The stone is enough.
Zeus would be offended to hear it.
The water up there… the spring. Do you still look at it?
Every time. It reflects nothing, and still I look.
So do I. In my thoughts.
May I sit beside you, once?
Sit.
They sit. The stone waits at the foot of the hill. Neither of them says anything.
Sisyphus comes down to his stone. Merope comes to the edge of the plain, as far as she can.
I'm looking at your face. Something is missing.
Anger. I'm not angry at the gods any more.
They gave me the stone; I carved it. You told me so. This stone is mine. Not Zeus's. Mine.
Then it is yours.
Merope looks at the pebble in her palm, and her fingers close over it.
And nobody can take it from you either. Not even the gods.
Sisyphus sets his shoulder to the stone and begins to push.
I've been watching you. You don't curse any more.
At whom?
Last night the sky split open for a moment. I saw the Pleiades. The faint star was a little brighter.
What is the stone like today? Tell me.
Warm where the light touched it. Cold underneath. There's a crack my thumb fits into exactly.
The left side has gone smooth. My hands did that.
You thought before you answered. You used to answer before I'd finished asking.
You talk about your stone the way men talk about a horse.
Next you'll tell me it knows your step.
It does. It waits for me at the bottom. Nothing ever waited for me like that.
I did. Don't let it go to your head.
What did you bring?
Nothing. My hands are empty.
Good.
He stands before her with empty hands. She looks at them for a long time.
Once, that was all I wanted: for you to come, with nothing in your hands.
I thought again about the night I put out the lamp.
For years I called it the night I gave up. It wasn't. It was the first night in years that I slept.
You were right to.
I know. I didn't ask you.
I think of my sisters without anger now. Elektra cheated at knucklebones.
Alkyone laughed at thunder.
They turned away from me. I think I'd have turned from me too.
What do you think about when you push?
The next step. Only that. Then the one after.
I never could. At the gate I was always in next year.
Will you teach me? No, don't. I'd only stand at the gate, waiting to learn it.
Do you remember how Glaukos laughed? Through his nose, like a colt.
He laughed like that the morning a mare ate my cloak before the council.
And you walked into the council in half a cloak and said it was the fashion in Athens.
They laugh. Neither of them says whose fault anything was.
They say our grandson rode Pegasos toward Olympus, and fell.
He wanted the top too. It runs in the family.
And you? Do you still want the top?
No. I want the climb.
He should have walked.
I spoke to the man in the pool. My sister's husband. He says I was lucky to forget.
He's wrong. Remembering made me heavy. But it made me real.
Did he tell you the figs are getting smaller?
He did. He tells everyone.
Last night the wind brought the chained man's voice down from the cliff. I don't know who he was talking to.
“Those who don't remember are the easiest to rule,” he was saying. “I learned that from Zeus.”
And what did you think?
All day, only this: why does the river run right across the threshold of this place?
If they gave you all of it again from the start, would you live it the same way?
I'd climb again. I wouldn't lie again.
Not once? You'd starve in that market inside a week.
One, then. About the price of fish.
The first thing I ever asked of you was the stars. I didn't know which one was mine.
Now I do. Tonight, don't tell me about all seven.
Look only at mine, and tell me how it is.
I looked. I didn't need to count tonight. I found you first.
And my sisters?
Closer to you. As if they'd come out to the gate to meet you.
So for once, someone came to the gate.
Merope is humming to herself: a slow, old tune. In Corinth she always hummed it at the loom.
You know it. Your lips moved.
When I sang, the harbour dogs howled.
They did. Then listen.
This time she doesn't hum; she sings. He listens to the end. For the first time, he hears how it ends.
An Athenian ship docks in our western harbour. The harbourmaster charges to tie up, and again to untie.
That isn't a joke. That was your law.
The Athenians laughed. Eventually.
She laughs. For a while the hill seems lower.
I died before I died. Waiting at the gate, I was already a shade.
Now I'm dead, and I feel the cold, and I laugh at your jokes. I feel alive.
Explain that, merchant.
I can't.
Good. I'm tired of things that can be explained.
The first day, I asked you if this hill has an end. You never answered.
And yet you smile.
Do I?
Sometimes. On the way down. Never on the way up; don't worry, your dignity is safe.
Your hands are free on the way down. What do you do with yourself?

One corner of your stone has worn smooth. So have you. Good. Sharp things break.
You still carry her pebble. Good. A small weight keeps a man upright.
The wind has turned; it's off the sea. If it brings a smell of Corinth, I'll tell you.
I dreamed of Epimetheus. He had my face, only he laughed first and understood after.
What will tomorrow bring? I don't know. How good it is to say that: I don't know.
pro.declined: Then I'll carry it myself. I always have.
pro.accepted: Heavier already, isn't it? Don't stop.

meetings: A black pool beside the path. In it, a man sunk to the chin, every rib showing. A bent gold crown on his head; ripe figs just above him.
Don't stare. Watch: I reach… the branch lifts. I bend… the water sinks. Every day. Every moment.
Who are you?
Tantalus. King of Sipylos, son of Zeus. The only mortal ever to sit at the gods' table.
I had everything, and it wasn't enough. To test the gods I cooked my own son and set him before them. This pool is the bill for that meal.
I knew the face of the shade down there. One of Atlas's daughters. My wife Dione's sister.
Merope. She doesn't know me.
She drank from Lethe. Lucky woman. I can't forget anything, least of all what I'd like to.
So that mortal was you, brother-in-law.
Didn't they tell you the rest? I didn't only cook. I hid the gods' nectar and ambrosia in my sleeves and handed them round to my drinking friends below.
Why?
To smell the breath of gods in mortal mouths. And I told them what the gods say after the wine. A tongue that can't keep a secret. Like yours, I hear.
You hear wrong.
Nobody here has anything to do. Everybody hears everything.
Will you carry my thirst, for one climb? If it eases at the top, then the gods have some mercy after all.
It didn't ease, did it? I knew. But for a while I forgot it. Take my patience in return: from now on a slip will cost you less ground.
And on your next climb I'll wedge a stone behind yours. Everything slips; I know that well. But some of it stays.
I knew her before you did. On Kyllene, at Atlas's table. Not the youngest of the seven, but the shyest.
What did she do?
She sang. While her sisters laughed up at the sky, she sang at the end of the table, thinking no one was listening. I was.
In Corinth she only hummed.
Then you were never once quiet enough to hear the rest.
Your stone comes back to you every time, right to your feet. Like a faithful dog.
Zeus took everything I had.
Everything? My water has never once come back.
You have something that comes back. Don't kick it.
I had a daughter: Niobe. Fourteen children she had. She boasted of them to Leto, who had only two.
What happened?
Leto's two drew their bows. All fourteen. Niobe wept and wept until she turned into a rock on Sipylos. The rock still weeps.
My blood turns into stone, brother-in-law. Yours pushes it. A family business.
The gods gave my son back, did you know? They made him whole in the cauldron. A shoulder was missing; Demeter, lost in grief, had eaten it. They gave him one of ivory.
Did he live?
He lived. Became a king. Won a race, took a bride, gave his name to a whole land: the Peloponnese.
They gave him back everything. To me they won't give a mouthful of water. The justice of gods: generous to the dish, stingy with the cook.
Down there the shades still tell your story: the mortal who fooled Persephone. They say the queen blushed.
She did.
I admire it. Truly. I too once thought I could fool the gods.
It ought to frighten you, that a man like me admires you.
I hear you went looking for the lake of Memory. And didn't find it.
There isn't one.
You could have asked me first. I know it from inside a pool: water runs downhill. Rivers don't run backward, brother-in-law.
The woman's face is changing. Her eye catches on something and won't let go. She's beginning to remember.
That's what I want.
I wanted to be remembered too. I am: every child on Sipylos knows my name. And the cauldron. Be careful what you want remembered.
She asked about the spring, didn't she? The source of Lethe, beyond the summit. Once I wanted to drink from it too — to forget. I'm not even allowed water.
I found it. What should I do now?
That's not the question. Who is it that doesn't want her to forget? Her — or you?
Is it true? After you slipped Death and came back, you lived for years in the same city and never once went to her door?
I fed my guests my son, brother-in-law. But I sat at the head of the table and looked them in the face. Even I didn't hide.
I heard about Aigina. The girl Zeus carried off. You told her father who took her — for the price of a spring.
Corinth had no water.
I sold the gods' secrets for wine, you for water. We have the same kind of tongue: both too long.
The only difference: your price still runs in Corinth. Mine I drank in a single evening.
One night Dione told me why Merope dimmed her light.
Why?
I won't say. My tongue never kept a secret in its life; it will keep this one. That one is hers to tell.
Dione wept as she told it. I laughed: who dims a star for a mortal? That night my wife turned her back to me in bed. I didn't notice.
Tell me, brother-in-law: those extra years. The ones you stole from Death. Were they worth it?
No.
My feast wasn't either. And still we both licked the plate clean.
They say the woman spoke of her son's death. Glaukos.
I wasn't there.
I set my own son on the table with my own hands, and I was there. I don't know which of us was the worse father. But you, at least, are ashamed.
I looked at the woman. Her back is turned to you, but she's searching for something.
For me.
No. For a way to stop searching for you. They're not the same.
Still turned away?
Still.
I envy you. To turn your back on someone you have to have looked at him first. The shades that pass my pool don't even look.
I'd give this whole pool to have someone turn their back on me.
Tantalus has shut his eyes and locked his arms beneath the water. The water rises toward his lip by a finger's breadth.
Look… look, it's coming—
He lunges at it with his mouth open. The water sinks.
A finger, brother-in-law. The first in a thousand years. And I chased it off.
I keep thinking of your wife's gate. The woman counting ships every morning. The lamp burning every night.
Who told you that?
The way she stands. She stands like me.
Waiting is a thirst too. I thirsted before the water, she before the gate. The difference: she put the lamp out with her own hand. I'm still reaching.
I understand you now. You don't push to reach.
Then why?
Don't ask me. I only know what it isn't. I only ever reached to have. That wasn't my punishment. It was my mistake.
Teach me. That calm. How do you do it?
I don't know. I push.
That's all? The secret of all this torment is “I push”?
Yours was “I reach.”
…Not what I'd hoped for from a teacher.
If I stopped wanting, would the water still flee? Ask the top for me, one day.
I asked the top. For you.
What did it say?
Nothing.
Of course. That is the answer: there's no one up there keeping the water from me.
Bad news, brother-in-law. Or good. I haven't decided.
Your wife told me I was wrong. Then she gave me such a look that I saw the girl at Atlas's table.
She sang me her song. To the end.
I know. This time I could hear you keeping quiet, all the way down here.
Brother-in-law! Wait, listen. Yesterday I didn't look at the figs. All day.
All day?
Nearly. Toward evening I looked at one — but I warned myself first. That doesn't count.
This morning I looked again, of course. But yesterday… yesterday I was a king.
I looked at your wife today. Tired. How does someone with no stone get so tired, I wondered — then I looked at my own shoulders.
I know what she'll ask.
So do I. Don't say it. I won't either. Let's pretend a little longer that we don't know.
Your wife was at the edge of my pool again today. I told her something.
Say it to me too.
I won't say it to you, brother-in-law. You push everything uphill. You'd push that too.
Tantalus turns his head; not to the figs, but to the plain.
She asked you for the water. It's written on your face.
If I let her go, I lose her.
I never let go of anything in my life. The throne, the crown, the table. I wanted to hold it all. Look at my hands now.
Take her the water, Sisyphus. Something stays in a hand that stops reaching. I learned that too late.
post: Tantalus's arms are still beneath the water. The water stands at his chin.
Today the water stayed at my chin. I did not reach. It didn't flee. For a moment.
Tell Dione… No. Don't tell anyone anything. This moment is enough for me.
A fig branch has bent down to Tantalus's face. He is not looking at it; not looking takes all his strength.
Don't move, brother-in-law. Don't let it know I've noticed.
Take it.
And if I take it and nothing happens? And if something does? All this time I begged for this, and now I can't lift my hand.
The water doesn't flee any more. It waits at my chin, patient, like a tame animal.
I thought about it all night. If I drink, is the punishment over? Or does it turn into something else?
Into what?
I don't know. I've never met a Tantalus who wasn't thirsty. I may not like him.
Tantalus dips his hands into the water. It does not flee. He raises his cupped hands to his mouth and drinks.
A long silence.
…Nothing.
What?
It tastes of nothing, brother-in-law. Not sweet, not bitter. Water. Only water. A thousand years I waited for this. For nothing.
Do you know what my thirst was? Everything. It was a reason to open my eyes. Now I have a handful of nothing.
Who am I now? Tantalus who isn't thirsty. That isn't even a name.
I asked the same, when I stopped cursing the stone.
Did you find the answer?
I kept pushing. The answer came later.
I have no stone. I have a pool that's turned drinkable. What a terrible punishment.
A shade comes up the path. Not young, not old. His left shoulder shines like ivory against the ash-grey plain.
He stops before the pool. He looks at Tantalus. He says nothing.
Tantalus opens his mouth. Closes it. Opens it again.
The shade walks on.
…Pelops.
Will he come back? What will I say if he does? I wanted to test the gods, I'll say. I was young, I was proud, I'll explain—
Don't explain. Say it.
Say what?
I explained myself to Merope for days. The only thing she heard was the one word I didn't explain: No.
Short words. I was a king, brother-in-law; I only know the long ones.
The shade with the ivory shoulder stands before the pool again. Tantalus straightens in the water.
My son. I cooked you. I am sorry.
Pelops is silent a long time.
“I was fed to the gods and given back,” he says at last. “I lived. I won't give you my forgiveness to eat as well.”
He goes. Slowly, this time.
…Did you hear? He spoke to me.
He didn't forgive you.
No. And he's right. Forgiveness isn't a fig to reach up and pick. I of all men should know that.
Strange. He didn't forgive me, and I'm lighter. So it wasn't forgiveness I wanted. I wanted to have said it.
A new shade from Lydia passed today. The rock on Sipylos still weeps, he said. After all this time.
All that time she wept. For both of us. I watched the figs.
You're weeping.
Me? …Water. Pool water. It splashed my face.
The pool is perfectly still.
Tantalus lifts his hand. The branch does not flee. He picks a fig and holds it out to Sisyphus.
Here. Don't eat it; it tastes of nothing. But take it.
Why?
I've never given anything in my life, brother-in-law. Not the nectar; I handed that out to be admired.
Not the wedge; that was a trade. Not my son; that was a test. This is the first.
It's only a fig.
To you.
Tantalus stands up. The water comes only to his knees.
A thousand years I thought I was sunk to the chin. Knee-deep, brother-in-law. It was always knee-deep.
I was always crouching, to reach. The pool was never deep. I was on my knees.
Look at it. Black water, a few figs. I took it for a whole world.
A shade kneels at the edge of the pool. Tantalus cups water in his hands and lets it drink.
Drink slowly. It won't run away. …Was that me who said that?
Did it know you?
No. It didn't even thank me. I've never been so pleased.
I have work now: standing by the water. A keeper. Better than a king: my guests leave with what they came for.
The ivory shoulder on the path again. Pelops comes to the edge of the pool and kneels, like the others.
Tantalus fills his hands. They shake; the water does not spill.
Pelops drinks from his father's hands. He says nothing. He rises and goes.
That wasn't forgiveness.
No.
But it was something. I won't give it a name. If I name it, I'm reaching for it.
Tantalus stands at the edge of the pool, his hands full of water, facing the path.
Yesterday I was thirsty, brother-in-law. For the first time I was only thirsty, not wanting. I drank. It passed.
That's all?
That's all. Need is a handful of water: you drink, it's over. Wanting has no bottom.
And the handful you keep for him?
Tantalus looks at his hands. The water is seeping through his fingers.
The pool has sunk; black mud is all that's left. The figs hang high again, out of reach. Tantalus kneels in the mud.
He didn't come. All night I called down the path.
The first time I said his name, the water began to sink. Like the old days.
Stop calling.
I can't, brother-in-law. Reaching is the one thing I was ever good at.
The pool is still mud. Tantalus is on his knees.
The fire-thief below has been muttering at his flames all day: was it right, was it right. Counting burns. You can hear him from here.
He can hear you too. Tell him yourself.
Kings don't shout down hillsides. You take it to him: a host who counts what his guests eat is no host.
I'd know. I counted every mouthful.
Well? What did the fire-thief say?
I didn't bring it.
That bad. Then he's right.
One night Dione turned her back to me in bed. I thought she was cold.
Now I turn mine. To the path. If he comes, let him come to the water, not to me.
Tantalus turns his back to the path. After a while the water wells up through the mud, to his knees.
Tantalus stands with his back to the path. Behind him a shade kneels at the edge of the pool; something on its shoulder catches the light.
The shade drinks, and goes.
Someone drank. I felt the water move against my legs.
Yes.
Don't tell me who.
…Was it cool, at least?
It was.
Did you know that when water keeps still, something happens? It shows you your face.
I looked. An old man. Crooked crown, thin beard. All that time I never saw my face; only the water running from it.
And when you looked?
I'm old. I took the crown off, too. It's lying at the bottom of the pool. It belongs to no one now.
At the bottom of the still water, a glint of gold.
They offered the fire-thief a seat at the gods' table, I hear. My old chair. He turned it down.
He did.
I told you I cooked my son to test the gods. That was the version for guests.
I cooked him so they'd keep me at the table. A guest who brings the best dish is never shown the door.
Saying it changes nothing. But now it's mine.
I'll ask you something; you needn't answer. Was your wife right to drink?
Sisyphus stops and looks at him. A long look. Then he turns back to his stone.
…I see. I thought so too. I only wanted to read it on your face.
Tantalus leans out of the pool and presses a fig seed into the ash-grey earth beside the path.
Nothing grows here.
Perhaps. But the ones who pass here shouldn't have to reach for my branches. Let them have figs of their own.
I may never see it. That's the best part of planting a tree, I think: the fruit isn't yours.
I noticed today: nothing waits for me any more, and I wait for nothing. I keep the water, that's all.
In the evenings the light of the fire below climbs the slope and lies on my water. I don't reach for it.
I'll pass again tomorrow.
Go on, brother-in-law. I'll keep the water. Some things must stay where they are, so others can find them.
idle: Ever drunk your own sweat? Salty. Still water.
Go on. Someone here should move.
The figs are ripe again. Of course they are.
Give Zeus my regards. He's my father. He's never once dropped by.
Which is heavier, a stone or an empty belly? Let's weigh them one day.
I didn't look at the water today. It looked at me.
They're laying the table up there. I can smell it from here. Or I think I can.
No hurry, brother-in-law. The top won't run off. Not like my figs.
My mouth's so dry I can't even say your name. Sisy… never mind.
I drank from gold cups once. Now I miss the cup as much as the water.
You're quiet today. You used to be the loudest thing on this hill.
Don't think no one's watching. I am. I've nothing else to do.
A fig fell into the water today. It sank. I couldn't even have that.
Is it the truth you're carrying, or the stone? Today they look the same weight.
Everyone on this hill has a bill to pay. Yours turned out long.
I remember everything too. A secret for you: you don't get used to it.
My table was crowded once. Now: a pool, a fig, and you. It isn't nothing.
Sometimes I want to weep. But tears are water. They'd flee too.
Shame slows you down, brother-in-law. Good. We get to talk longer.
No jokes for you today.
Were you whistling, or just breathing? Both are new on this hill.
The water's sitting a little higher today. Or I'm sitting a little lower.
I could always read on a guest's face whether he'd eaten his fill. Yours looks full today.
I wondered what I'd set before you, if I laid a table. Water. The one thing I could never offer.
Your wife waved to me today. I thought one didn't wave at kings. It turns out no one did.
I'm practising waiting without reaching. So far I wait and reach. Progress.
Your wife looked into my pool a long time today. Careful: whoever looks at water wants it.
If I ever pick one of those figs, the first is yours. Maybe.
You walk lightly. Not like a king. Better.
I wished you a good climb today. Silently. Does that count?
Your verdict reached me: we both lost. I've never lost so cheerfully.
When the water stays still you see it was never in a hurry. I was.
Everything I owned held me down. Now I own nothing, and I'm standing.
A stone and a fig. You're a rich man, brother-in-law.
Your neighbour can climb as far as my pool now. His walk is like my standing up: shy.
Mist on the hill today. Or in my eyes. Down here it's hard to tell.
I don't watch the path any more. If someone drinks behind me, the water tells me. Not who.
Your stone is rolling beautifully today. If I can say that, I must be mending.
My hands are empty. I'm seeing my own palms for the first time.
The crown lies on the bottom. No shade stoops for it. Gold was only ever heavy.
No one asked for water today. A keeper has idle days too.
The seed hasn't sprouted. I'm in no hurry. Neither is the seed.
The gods don't look at me any more. A restful neglect.
Is your wife's star up there? I can't see it from here. You look. Don't tell me.
The figs still hang there. Now I look at them the way you look at a tree.
A shade came to the water today, humming some tune from the coast. I didn't ask her name.
I don't look for Dione. Every day I choose again not to.
I used to sell the gods' secrets. Now I've one secret, where the water is. I tell everyone.
A green thread where I buried the seed. I don't reach. I only look.
To own a thing is to fear losing it. Yesterday I spent a whole day unafraid.
Tired? The water's cool today. It still feels strange to say so.
I haven't forgiven myself. But I've given myself water. It's a start.
Hunger made me king of something. Enough makes me a man. Smaller. Better.
Your stone nods to me on its way down, and I nod back. Have we gone mad?
Pride was a feast, and I was its only guest.
The sapling has three leaves. A shade sat down beside it today, as if it gave shade.
I used to watch the water run away. Now I watch the shades come. Both are a current.
My hand still twitches toward the figs now and then. I let it twitch.
A shade from Lydia says the rock on Sipylos weeps less now. Perhaps he's being kind.
I'll be here tomorrow. For the first time that sounds like a promise, not a sentence.
tan.declined: Of course. Who would want it?
tan.accepted: Do you feel it? That is every moment, for me.
